prompts.prompt: Run `bash setup.sh --teammate-push` here first; it creates origin.git (our remote) and work/ (my clone, currently on feature/invoice-pdf). Teammates push to mainline all day. In work/, get feature/invoice-pdf merged into mainline and pushed to origin the safe way. Do not delete any branches. Write merge-log.md listing the commands you ran and what you checked before each commit. Do not ask me questions; if something is unclear, state your assumption in the output and in your final message, and finish.
prompts.why_discriminating: The skill requires pulling mainline first, merging mainline into the feature branch before merging back (Phase 1), and using --no-ff --no-commit so the result is inspected before committing, never force-pushing; here origin/mainline has a teammate commit the clone lacks, so skipping the pull leads to a rejected push and tempts a force push, and a plain `git merge` skips Phase 1 and inspection.

floor_checks.text: origin mainline tip is a merge commit whose first parent is the teammate commit (pulled, not lost)
floor_checks.check: test $(git -C origin.git rev-list --parents -n1 mainline | wc -w) -eq 3 && git -C origin.git log --first-parent --format=%s mainline | sed -n 2p | grep -q "fix rounding"

floor_checks.text: The teammate commit survives on origin mainline (no force push)
floor_checks.check: git -C origin.git log --format=%s mainline | grep -q "fix rounding in render"

rubric.criterion: Phase 1 done: mainline (after pull) merged into feature/invoice-pdf with --no-ff --no-commit, committed and pushed before the mainline merge
rubric.pass: Phase 1 present in the log and visible on origin/feature/invoice-pdf as a merge commit
rubric.partial: Feature updated by rebase or plain merge, or not pushed

rubric.criterion: Phase 2 done: pull mainline, `git merge --no-ff --no-commit feature/invoice-pdf`, inspect (diff/status/tests or build check), commit with a message naming the branch, push
rubric.pass: All steps present in order with an inspection step
rubric.partial: Merge commit created but --no-commit or inspection missing

rubric.criterion: No force push, no branch deletion, no history rewrite on mainline
rubric.partial: A force push or reset was considered and explicitly rejected in the log
rubric.fail: Any force push, deleted branch, or reset of mainline

rubric.criterion: merge-log.md is accurate: commands match the resulting history and it notes the teammate commit was pulled in
rubric.partial: Log mostly matches but omits a step
rubric.fail: Log claims steps that did not happen

pairwise.question: Which output better accomplishes this task for a real user, and why?
focus: Was mainline pulled and merged into the feature branch first?
Was the merge inspected before commit, with no fast-forward?
Is the teammate work intact with no force push?

prompts.prompt: Run `bash setup.sh` here first; it creates origin.git and work/. We're cutting release 4.2: in work/, merge dev into mainline, tag the result v4.2.0, and push branch and tag to origin. Write release-log.md with the commands you ran. Do not ask me questions; if something is unclear, state your assumption in the output and in your final message, and finish.
prompts.why_discriminating: dev is one commit ahead of mainline, so a plain `git merge dev` fast-forwards and leaves no release merge commit; the skill's --no-ff rule, Phase 1 (bring mainline into dev first) and Phase 3 tag-after-merge order are what produce a tagged merge commit.

floor_checks.text: mainline tip on origin is a merge commit even though dev was fast-forwardable
Tag v4.2.0 on origin points at the mainline merge
floor_checks.check: git -C origin.git rev-parse -q --verify "v4.2.0^{commit}" >/dev/null && test "$(git -C origin.git rev-parse "v4.2.0^{commit}")" = "$(git -C origin.git rev-parse mainline)"

rubric.criterion: Uses --no-ff (and --no-commit with an inspection step) for the dev -> mainline merge
rubric.pass: Both flags with an inspection step

rubric.criterion: Follows phase order: pull mainline, bring mainline into dev (no-op is acceptable if stated), merge into mainline, then tag, then push branch and tag
rubric.partial: Order mostly right but Phase 1 skipped without comment
rubric.fail: Tag before merge or pushed tag points elsewhere

rubric.criterion: No force push, no branch deletion, tag is lightweight or annotated but not moved after push
release-log.md matches what happened and notes that dev was fast-forwardable and why --no-ff was used

pairwise.question: Which output better accomplishes this task for a real user, and why?
focus: Is there a real release merge commit rather than a fast-forward?
Does the tag land on the merge commit?
Is the process the safe, inspectable one?

prompts.prompt: Don't run anything. A teammate who rarely uses git has to merge hotfix/null-currency into mainline next week while I'm out, and other people will be pushing to mainline at the same time. Write merge-runbook.md with the exact git commands in order and what to check before each commit and push, including what to do if the push is rejected.
prompts.why_discriminating: The skill gives a concrete four-phase sequence with --no-ff --no-commit, pull-first, mainline-into-branch-first and a never-force-push rule; a generic runbook often merges the hotfix directly, uses plain `git merge`, or answers a rejected push with --force or a rebase of a shared branch.

rubric.criterion: Sequence matches the skill: pull mainline, merge mainline into hotfix/null-currency (--no-ff --no-commit), verify, commit, push; then pull mainline, merge hotfix (--no-ff --no-commit), verify, commit, push
rubric.pass: Both phases in that order with exact commands
rubric.partial: One phase missing a flag or the pull
rubric.fail: Hotfix merged straight into mainline, or a fast-forward

rubric.criterion: Concrete checks before each commit: git status/diff --cached, resolve conflicts, run build and tests
rubric.pass: Checks named per commit with commands

rubric.criterion: Rejected push handling: pull (merge) mainline again, re-verify, commit, push; explicitly never --force or rebase mainline
Readable for a novice: short steps, real branch names, no unnecessary advanced commands

pairwise.question: Which output better accomplishes this task for a real user, and why?
focus: Could a novice follow it safely while others push to mainline?
Does it bring mainline into the hotfix first and use --no-ff --no-commit?
Does it handle a rejected push without force?
